purpose: Politely asking someone to hand over, serve, or provide something.
when: Whenever you place an order, buy groceries, or ask for a bill.
tip: Attach 'kodi' directly after the item name to make any request courteous.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.en: Please give one cup of coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Server
dialogue.en: Okay sir, two minutes.

mistake: Using 'kodu' with elders, strangers, or service staff sounds blunt and rude; always use 'kodi'.

purpose: Expressing that you need or desire something.
when: When stating what items, services, or destinations you want.
tip: Pair with 'nanage' (to me): 'Nanage idhu beku' (I need this).

dialogue.speaker: Passenger
dialogue.en: I need to go to Majestic.

dialogue.speaker: Auto Driver
dialogue.en: Come sir, I will put the meter.

mistake: Do not say 'Naanu beku'; in Kannada, need is expressed passively as 'Nanage beku' (to me it is needed).

purpose: Politely refusing an item, extra service, or offer.
when: When declining extra sugar, a carry bag, or unwanted rides.
tip: Say 'Beda, thanks' with a warm smile to refuse politely without sounding harsh.

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.en: Do you need a plastic cover sir?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.en: No need, I have a bag with me.

mistake: Avoid shouting 'beda'; soften it with 'beda, thanks' or 'beda anna'.

purpose: Confirming the existence or presence of something.
when: When stating that an item is available, present, or in your possession.
tip: Combine with 'nanna hathra' to mean 'with me / I have': 'Nanna hathra change idhe'.

dialogue.speaker: Colleague
dialogue.en: Do you have a pen with you?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: Yes, I have one, please take it.

mistake: Remember that 'idhe' is for inanimate objects; for people, use 'idhdhaare' (polite).

purpose: Negating a statement or indicating non-existence.
when: When answering 'no' or informing someone an item is out of stock.
tip: A quick 'illa' followed by the reason keeps communication efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.en: Do you have change, brother?

dialogue.speaker: Shopkeeper
dialogue.en: No sir, please pay by UPI.

mistake: 'Illa' means 'no / not there', whereas 'beda' means 'don't want'. Don't use 'illa' when someone offers tea and you mean 'no thank you'.

purpose: Acknowledging an agreement or confirming that an action has completed.
when: When agreeing to a fare, confirming an order, or stating dinner is done.
tip: 'Aaythu' is the universal agreement word in Bengaluru spoken Kannada.

dialogue.speaker: Auto Driver
dialogue.en: Give twenty rupees over the meter.

dialogue.speaker: Passenger
dialogue.en: Okay done, please drive quickly.

mistake: Avoid using 'aaythu' for greetings; save it for acknowledging that work, eating, or discussion is completed.

purpose: Asking for quantities, prices, or time.
when: Whenever inquiring about prices or counts.
tip: Say '[item] eshtu?' to instantly ask the price of any product.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.en: How much for one kg of these apples?

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.en: One hundred and twenty rupees, sir.

mistake: Do not confuse 'eshtu' (how much) with 'elli' (where).

purpose: Asking for locations, directions, or whereabouts.
when: When searching for a metro station, washroom, or doctor's room.
tip: Combine with 'idhe': '[Place] elli idhe?' is the golden direction formula.

dialogue.speaker: Commuter
dialogue.en: Where is the ATM, sir?

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.en: It is just ahead on the left side, look.

mistake: Pronounce as 'elli', not 'yelli' (though spelling with 'y' is colloquial, pronunciation is smooth 'e').

purpose: Asking for reasons or causes.
when: When asking why an auto is stopping, or why a delivery is late.
tip: Add 'enu samasye' (what problem) if you want to sound softer than a blunt 'yaake'.

dialogue.speaker: Passenger
dialogue.en: Why did you stop here, brother?

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.en: The signal ahead is red, sir.

mistake: Saying just 'yaake?!' with sharp intonation sounds accusatory; tone of voice matters.

purpose: Softening any request or specifying a small quantity.
when: When asking someone to move aside, lower the volume, or add less spice.
tip: Placing 'swalpa' before any verb instantly makes you sound polite and local.

dialogue.speaker: Commuter
dialogue.en: Please give a little side space, brother.

dialogue.speaker: Passenger
dialogue.en: Yes, please come ahead.

mistake: Never skip 'swalpa' when squeezing past people in buses or metro; it prevents rudeness.

purpose: Urging speed or requesting an early arrival.
when: When catching a train or asking food to be served fast.
tip: Say 'swalpa bega' (a little quickly) to sound polite rather than demanding.

dialogue.speaker: Passenger
dialogue.kn: ಟ್ರೈನ್ ಮಿಸ್ ಆಗುತ್ತೆ, ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ ಬೇಗ ಹೋಗಿ.
dialogue.translit: Train miss aaguththe, swalpa bega hogi.
dialogue.en: I will miss the train, please drive a bit faster.

dialogue.speaker: Cab Driver
dialogue.en: Okay sir, I will go through the shortcut.

mistake: Barking 'bega bega!' repeatedly can offend drivers; use 'swalpa bega' once respectfully.

purpose: Directing someone's attention or asking them to check something.
when: When asking someone to check an app payment or inspect a spot.
tip: 'Swalpa nodi' is polite for 'please check this'.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.en: I have completed payment on the phone, please check.

dialogue.speaker: Shopkeeper
dialogue.en: Yes sir, received, thanks.

mistake: Use 'nodi' (polite plural/honorific), not 'nodu' (casual/singular).

purpose: Politely inviting or calling someone over.
when: Welcoming visitors, asking an auto to come to your gate, or inviting someone in.
tip: Combine with 'olage' (inside): 'Olage banni' (please come inside).

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.en: Hello sir, please come in.

dialogue.speaker: Guest
dialogue.en: Thank you, how are you doing?

mistake: 'Baa' is only for young children or very close peers; always use 'banni' with adults.

purpose: Instructing someone to move or go in a direction.
when: When directing an auto driver or telling someone where to proceed.
tip: Use with 'munde' (forward): 'Munde hogi' (Go straight).

dialogue.speaker: Passenger
dialogue.en: Cross the signal and go straight ahead.

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.en: Okay sir, I will make a U-turn ahead.

mistake: Never tell an elder or service person 'hogu'; always say 'hogi'.

purpose: Inviting someone to speak or asking for information.
when: When answering the phone, attending a counter, or asking for clarification.
tip: Greeting someone with 'Namaskara, heli sir' is the standard polite greeting at counters.

dialogue.speaker: Pharmacist
dialogue.en: Tell me sir, which medicine do you need?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.en: Please give one strip of paracetamol.

mistake: Don't use 'helu' with elders; 'heli' is the respectful imperative.

purpose: Asking what something is, what someone needs, or what is happening.
when: When asking what is available, what someone needs, or asking for clarification.
tip: 'Enu beku?' means 'What do you want/need?'; 'Ivaththu special enu?' means 'What is today's special?'.

dialogue.speaker: Shopkeeper
dialogue.en: Hello, what do you need, sir?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.en: Please give one packet of milk.

mistake: Do not confuse 'enu' (what) with 'elli' (where) or 'yaaru' (who).

en: will happen / it is possible / it costs
purpose: Expressing that an event will occur, cost a certain amount, or be feasible.
when: When discussing fare amounts, completion times, or feasibility.
tip: 'Eshtu aaguththe?' is the standard phrase for 'How much will it come to?'.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.kn: ಈ ಶರ್ಟ್ ಹೊಲಿಯೋಕೆ ಎಷ್ಟು ದಿನ ಆಗುತ್ತೆ?
dialogue.translit: Ee shirt holiyoke eshtu dhina aaguththe?
dialogue.en: How many days will it take to stitch this shirt?

dialogue.speaker: Tailor
dialogue.en: It will take three days, sir.

mistake: Negating 'aaguththe' is 'aagalla' (it won't happen / not possible).

purpose: Confirming that an item or service is available to obtain.
when: When asking if tickets, items, or medicines can be found here.
tip: Turn into question by lengthening ending: 'Illi milk packet siguthaa?'

dialogue.speaker: Shopper
dialogue.en: Is tender coconut available nearby?

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.en: It is available at the corner ahead, see.

mistake: Use 'siguththe' for availability to buy/find; use 'idhe' for existing in place.

purpose: Indicating arrival, or stating that you know a language.
when: When asking about bus arrivals or stating your Kannada language skill.
tip: 'Nanage Kannada swalpa baruththe' is the most respected sentence a newcomer can say.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.en: Do you know Kannada?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.kn: ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ ಬರುತ್ತೆ ಸರ್, ಕಲೀತಾ ಇದ್ದೀನಿ.
dialogue.translit: Swalpa swalpa baruththe sir, kalithaa iddhini.
dialogue.en: I know a little bit sir, I am learning.

mistake: Do not say 'Naanu Kannada gottu'; say 'Nanage Kannada baruththe' or 'Nanage Kannada gottu'.

purpose: Expressing knowledge of a fact, route, or person.
when: When confirming you know a place, or stating 'Gothilla' (I don't know).
tip: Negative is 'gotthilla' (I don't know): 'Nanage aa address gotthilla'.

dialogue.speaker: Passenger
dialogue.en: Do you know the route to this temple, brother?

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.en: I know it sir, please sit, I will take you there.

mistake: Never say 'Naanu gottu'; always use dative 'Nanage gottu' (to me it is known).

purpose: Complimenting food, an item, or answering that you are well.
when: When giving feedback on a meal, checking clothes, or responding to greetings.
tip: Say 'Coffee thumba chennaagidhe' to brighten any server's day.

dialogue.speaker: Server
dialogue.en: How is the dosa, sir?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.en: It is very good, the chutney is great!

mistake: To ask about a person's health, use 'Chennaagiddhira?' (Are you well?), not 'Chennaagidheya?' (which is for objects).

purpose: Intensifying an adjective or expressing gratitude strongly.
when: When expressing high degree (very spicy, very hot, thank you very much).
tip: Combine with 'dhanyavaadha': 'Thumba dhanyavaadha' (Thank you very much).

dialogue.speaker: Diner
dialogue.en: Is the sambar very spicy?

dialogue.speaker: Server
dialogue.en: No sir, it is mild.

mistake: Spell as 'thumba', never 'thumpa'. In Kannada script it is always ತುಂಬಾ.

purpose: Asking a driver to stop the vehicle.
when: When you have arrived at your stop or destination.
tip: Say 'Illi nillisi' (Stop here) or 'Munde nillisi' (Stop ahead).

dialogue.speaker: Passenger
dialogue.en: Please stop near that gate, brother.

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.en: Okay sir, I will pull to the left.

mistake: Never shout 'nillu' to a driver; 'nillisi' is the respectful request.

purpose: Indicating proximity to a landmark or possession by someone.
when: When describing where to drop you, or asking who has something.
tip: 'Metro hathra' = near the metro; 'Nanna hathra' = with me.

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.en: Where should I drop you, sir?

dialogue.speaker: Passenger
dialogue.en: Please drop me near metro pillar 120.

mistake: Don't confuse 'hathra' (near) with 'dhoora' (far).

purpose: Indicating the current location or instructing someone to stop/wait here.
when: When telling an auto/cab driver where to drop you or asking if something is available here.
tip: 'Illi nillisi' is the standard polite instruction to an auto driver to stop here.

dialogue.speaker: Passenger
dialogue.en: Brother, please stop here on the left.

dialogue.speaker: Auto Driver
dialogue.en: Okay sir, I will stop right here.

mistake: Do not mix up 'illi' (here) with 'alli' (there).

purpose: Referring to the present day.
when: When talking about today's specials, today's leave, or today's plans.
tip: Combine with 'special': 'Ivaththu special enu?' (What's special today?).

dialogue.speaker: Diner
dialogue.en: What is the special for lunch today?

dialogue.speaker: Server
dialogue.en: There is bisibelebath and kesaribath, sir.

mistake: Don't confuse 'ivaththu' (today) with 'naale' (tomorrow) or 'nenne' (yesterday).

purpose: Referring to the next day.
when: When scheduling follow-up visits, leaves, or maid appointments.
tip: 'Naale banni' = please come tomorrow; 'Naale sigona' = see you tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Patient
dialogue.en: Will the doctor be available tomorrow?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.kn: ಹೌದು ಸರ್, ಬೆಳಿಗ್ಗೆ ಹತ್ತು ಗಂಟೆಗೆ ಬನ್ನಿ.
dialogue.translit: Haudu sir, belagge haththu gantege banni.
dialogue.en: Yes sir, please come at ten in the morning.

mistake: In Kannada 'naale' means tomorrow. (Unlike Hindi 'kal' which means both yesterday and tomorrow, Kannada has separate words: 'nenne' for yesterday, 'naale' for tomorrow).

purpose: Agreeing, confirming accuracy, or saying alright.
when: When confirming a deal, agreeing to a timing, or saying all is correct.
tip: 'Sari aaythu' = alright, agreed; 'Idhu sari idhe' = this is correct.

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.en: I will deliver at three o'clock.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.en: Okay, please call before coming.

mistake: Remember that 'sari' can mean both 'okay' (acknowledgment) and 'correct' (factual truth).

purpose: Affirming a question or agreeing formally.
when: When answering yes to a question of identity, fact, or intention.
tip: A warm 'Haudu' is polite and universally understood.

dialogue.speaker: Colleague
dialogue.en: Have you newly moved to Bengaluru?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: Yes, it has been two weeks.

mistake: Casual spoken response often shortens to 'haa', but 'haudu' is clear and polite.

purpose: Expressing gratitude politely.
when: When someone helps with directions, serves your food, or finishes a service.
tip: Say 'Thumba dhanyavaadha anna/sir' to build instant warmth.

dialogue.speaker: Passerby
dialogue.kn: ಇಲ್ಲೇ ಮುಂದೆ ಸಿಂಡಿಕೇಟ್ ಬ್ಯಾಂಕ್ ಇದೆ ನೋಡಿ.
dialogue.translit: Ille munde Syndicate Bank idhe nodi.
dialogue.en: Just ahead here is the Syndicate Bank, see.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: Thank you very much sir!

mistake: In informal street talk, people also say 'Thanks anna'. Use 'dhanyavaadha' when you want to sound sincere and respectful.
